title: When I dance, I dance
hookLine: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep (Essays 3.13)
carry: be wholly in what you do; drift, return

cards: Dinner is on the table, the phone is next to the plate, the news murmurs in the other room, and half your mind is already in tomorrow's meeting. Afterward, you could hardly say what you ate.
Montaigne, in the last essay of his book, called Of experience, describes another way of being at the table, on the dance floor, in bed at night.
The sentence could hardly be plainer: when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep.

teach.b: First, the sentence. It sounds almost too obvious. Of course when you dance, you dance.
But Montaigne means it as a discipline: when he does a thing, he tries to be wholly in it, not half there and half somewhere else. Second, the orchard. He doesn't pretend to be perfect at it.
Walking alone in a beautiful orchard, he says, his thoughts sometimes drift to far-away matters for part of the time.
For the other part, he brings them back: to the walk, the orchard, the sweetness of being alone there, and to himself. Drift, and return. That's the whole skill.
Nature, he says, has made the actions it requires of us pleasant: eating, sleeping, resting. To rush them, or look down on them as beneath a serious mind, misses something nature gave on purpose.

He's suspicious of people who treat a good meal as a waste of time. Fourth, the great men. Even generals and rulers he admired, he points out, found time for ordinary pleasures in the middle of great affairs.
Being wholly present wasn't a distraction from serious life; it was part of living it well.
Washing a cup, hugging a child at the door: when you wash, wash. When you hug, hug.

how: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line from Of experience, when I dance, I dance; when I sleep, I sleep, as a picture of giving full attention to ordinary acts.

o: Montaigne's love of dancing at grand court balls
do one thing wholly, and come back when you drift
a rule to finish every chore before resting

s: Montaigne claims his mind never wanders
in the orchard his thoughts drift for part of the time, and he brings them back.
he says nature made the actions it requires of us pleasant
eating, sleeping and resting are given to us to enjoy, not rush.
he says serious people should skip pleasures to save time
he's suspicious of that, and notes great men who enjoyed ordinary pleasures amid great affairs.

games.q: you're walking in a lovely orchard, like Montaigne, and your mind drifts to tomorrow's problems. what does he do?
o: give up on the walk and go solve the problems.
let them drift for a while, then bring them back to the orchard.
force himself never to think of anything else.
games.why: he admits his thoughts wander part of the time; the other part, he brings them back to the walk and to himself.

practice: When you breathe in, breathe in; when you breathe out, breathe out. Your mind will wander, the way Montaigne's did in the orchard, and when you notice, don't scold it: bring it back to the breath, the chair, this room, yourself.
Drift and return, as many times as it takes.

wordCard.voice: When I dance. Montaigne's short rule for being wholly in what you're doing, and coming back when you drift. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: be wholly in what you do; drift, return. When the mind wanders off, the orchard is still there to come back to. I'll be here tomorrow.
